items.title: Cybersecurity in Banking: Challenges and How to Overcome Them in 2027
items.summary: Key Takeaways Banks face evolving cyber threats, including ransomware, phishing, credential theft, supply chain attacks, and AI-powered impersonation. Effective banking cybersecurity requires continuous monitoring, strong identity controls, network visibility, and rapid incident response. Cloud security, third-party risk management, and compliance with applicable banking cybersecurity regulations are essential to protecting sensitive financial data. XDR, network inspection, and deception technology can help security teams detect suspicious activity, investigate threats, and reduce visibility gaps. Regular security assessments, employee awareness training, tested recovery plans, and measurable performance indicators help banks strengthen cyber resilience and protect customer trust. Why $16 Trillion in Bank Assets Became Cybercriminals' Ultimate Prize Banks manage vast amounts of sensitive financial data, customer information, and transaction records, making them attractive targets for cybercriminals. With financial institutions responsible for protecting trillions of dollars in assets, cybersecurity in banking has become a critical operational priority rather than just another item on a risk management checklist. The top cybersecurity threats to banks include ransomware, advanced persistent threats (APTs) , phishing, credential theft, supply chain attacks, and attacks targeting cloud infrastructure. Criminals are also using AI-generated deepfakes and automated attack techniques to impersonate customers and employees, bypass authentication controls, and exploit security gaps. The consequences extend beyond financial losses. Cybersecurity breaches in banking can expose customer data, disrupt transactions, compromise critical banking services, trigger regulatory scrutiny, and damage customer trust. Because financial institutions rely on interconnected networks, third-party providers, and digital banking platforms, a breach in one part of the ecosystem can create risks for others. Effective banking cybersecurity requires a combination of proactive threat detection , strong identity and access controls, continuous asset visibility, employee awareness, and tested incident response plans. Banks must also adapt their security programs to evolving banking cybersecurity regulations and emerging technologies to protect their operations and maintain customer confidence. Challenge #1: Top Cybersecurity Threats to Banks and Evolving Attack Vectors Banks face an evolving range of cyber threats, including advanced persistent threats (APTs), ransomware, phishing, credential theft, and attacks targeting online banking services. AI-generated deepfakes can help criminals impersonate customers, executives, or vendors, while mobile banking trojans can steal credentials and intercept authentication codes. Attackers also exploit weak passwords, unpatched systems, and third-party software vulnerabilities to gain unauthorized access. Common methods used to breach bank data include phishing, social engineering, brute-force attacks , stolen credentials, malware, software vulnerability exploitation, and supply chain compromises. Criminals may also use synthetic identities to bypass Know Your Customer (KYC) checks and facilitate financial fraud. Ransomware-as-a-service has lowered the technical barriers to launching attacks, enabling more criminal groups to target financial institutions. These cybersecurity risks for banks require defenses that identify suspicious activity across endpoints, networks, identities, and applications. Traditional security tools may miss attacks involving legitimate credentials or activity spread across multiple systems. Effective cybersecurity for banks therefore combines continuous monitoring, behavioral analysis, strong identity controls, and rapid incident response. Defending Data Breaches in Financial Institutions with Fidelis Elevate ® The Blind Spots That Keep CISOs Awake Blueprint of a Better Defense Stopping Data Theft Before It Happens Read Guide Banks can strengthen threat detection by correlating signals across multiple stages of an attack. Extended Detection and Response (XDR) platforms such as Fidelis Elevate ® help security teams connect related events and investigate suspicious activity. Fidelis Network ® provides network visibility and Deep Session Inspection to help uncover threats across supported ports and protocols, including suspicious activity within complex traffic and encrypted communications where inspection is supported. Together, these capabilities support real-time cyber threat detection and prevention in banking, helping security teams identify suspicious behavior earlier and respond before an incident causes wider disruption. Zero Trust Architecture further strengthens cybersecurity for banking by continuously verifying users, devices, and access requests rather than automatically trusting activity inside the network. When combined with XDR and continuous monitoring, Zero Trust helps financial institutions limit unauthorized access and identify potentially compromised accounts or devices. Challenge #2:Cloud Infrastructure and Supply Chain Vulnerabilities Digital transformation and cloud storage boost efficiency but create new entry points for attackers. Modern financial systems span multiple platforms with dozens of third-party vendors—each one a potential backdoor. Supply chain attacks target weaker vendor systems as stepping stones toward core banking operations. Cloud adoption introduces additional security risks. Misconfigured storage, overly permissive access controls, and insufficiently secured environments can expose sensitive information. Hybrid cloud environments increase complexity, making consistent security controls, visibility, and governance essential throughout migration and ongoing operations. Banks should integrate security reviews into cloud deployment and maintenance processes to identify and address weaknesses before they are exploited. Successful cybersecurity for banks depends on consistent security controls across on-premises infrastructure, cloud environments, and third-party services. Financial institutions should assess vendor access, enforce least-privilege permissions, review contractual security obligations, and continuously monitor connections to critical systems. Regular cloud configuration reviews and third-party risk assessments help identify weaknesses before attackers exploit them. These measures are especially important for cybersecurity for community banks, which may operate with smaller security teams and limited budgets. Community banks can prioritize essential controls such as multifactor authentication, secure backups, vulnerability management , centralized logging, and managed security services where appropriate. Cybersecurity risk management software for community banks can help consolidate risk assessments, track remediation, document controls, and support compliance activities, making it easier to manage cybersecurity risks and maintain audit evidence. Terrain mapping adds visibility by identifying managed and unmanaged assets across cloud and on-premises environments. Fidelis Elevate ® supports continuous asset discovery and risk profiling , helping security teams identify shadow IT, understand their attack surface, and prioritize protection based on risk. This visibility supports more informed security decisions across complex banking environments. Challenge #3: Banking Cybersecurity Regulations and Compliance Frameworks Banking cybersecurity regulations and supervisory expectations require financial institutions to demonstrate that they can identify, manage, and respond to cyber risks. The Federal Financial Institutions Examination Council (FFIEC) Cybersecurity Assessment Tool sunset on August 31, 2025, so institutions that previously relied on it should review alternative approaches to assessing cybersecurity maturity and risk. Applicable privacy requirements, including the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA), may also affect banks depending on their operations and the customers they serve. Compliance obligations vary by jurisdiction, institution type, and the systems involved. In the United States, the federal banking agencies’ Computer-Security Incident Notification Rule generally requires a banking organization to notify its primary federal regulator as soon as possible and no later than 36 hours after determining that a qualifying computer-security incident has occurred. Institutions must understand which requirements apply to them and maintain documented processes for escalation, reporting, and recovery. A structured compliance program helps financial institutions align security controls with applicable regulations and recognized frameworks. Relevant resources include the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, CIS Controls, and MITRE ATT&CK , which support different aspects of risk management, control implementation, and threat analysis. These resources serve different purposes: regulatory compliance, control implementation, and threat analysis should be coordinated rather than treated as interchangeable. Automated compliance tracking can help teams document controls, collect evidence, identify gaps, and monitor remediation. Fidelis Elevate ® supports threat detection and investigation, while mapping detected activity to MITRE ATT&CK can help security teams understand adversary techniques and communicate threat coverage. Compliance reporting should still be validated against the specific regulatory requirements that apply to each institution. Challenge #4: Human Factor Vulnerabilities and Social Engineering Human error, phishing, social engineering , and insider misuse remain important challenges in banking cybersecurity. Attackers may impersonate bank executives, customers, or vendors through convincing emails, messages, and AI-generated voice or video. Stolen credentials and synthetic identities can also be used to bypass weak authentication processes and facilitate unauthorized access to banking systems. The impact of cybersecurity incidents on banking customers and institutions can be significant. Customers may face financial fraud, exposure of personal information, identity theft, and interrupted access to banking services. Institutions may experience direct financial losses, incident response expenses, operational downtime, regulatory scrutiny, and reputational damage. The severity depends on the type of incident, the data affected, and how quickly the institution contains the threat. Alert fatigue can make it harder for security teams to identify genuine threats among large volumes of alerts. Banks can strengthen their defenses by enforcing multifactor authentication, applying least-privilege access, training employees to recognize phishing and deepfake-enabled impersonation, and regularly testing incident response procedures . Behavioral monitoring can help identify unusual access patterns, while centralized threat detection helps investigators connect related events across systems. These cybersecurity measures for banks are most effective when supported by clear escalation procedures and continuous review. Fidelis Elevate ® helps correlate security signals across attack stages, giving analysts contextual information to investigate suspicious activity and prioritize credible threats. This can reduce unnecessary investigation effort, although alert quality and false-positive reduction depend on configuration, data coverage, and ongoing tuning. Challenge #5: Operational Resilience, Cybersecurity Breaches, and Business Continuity Distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks , ransomware, and destructive malware can disrupt banking operations, delay transactions, and limit access to online and mobile banking services. The consequences of cybersecurity breaches in banking extend beyond the affected institution. These cybersecurity breaches banking risks can affect customers, payment systems, third-party providers, and the wider financial ecosystem. A serious breach can expose sensitive financial information, compromise transaction integrity, generate recovery costs, and undermine customer confidence. Financial institutions should therefore prepare for both data compromise and service disruption. Tested backup and recovery procedures, network segmentation , continuous monitoring, incident response exercises, and clearly assigned recovery responsibilities help banks maintain critical services and restore operations after an attack. Effective operational resilience combines intrusion detection and prevention, data loss prevention , continuous security monitoring, and tested incident response plans. Security operations teams need clear procedures for investigating alerts, containing compromised systems, restoring services, and communicating with relevant stakeholders. Banks should also test recovery plans against realistic scenarios, including ransomware, third-party outages, and disruptions to critical infrastructure. Deception technology provides an additional layer of defense by deploying decoys and breadcrumbs that can reveal unauthorized activity. Fidelis Deception ® helps security teams observe attacker behavior and gather intelligence on attempted intrusions. Combined with network visibility and threat detection, this approach can support earlier investigation and more informed incident response. Challenge #6: Banking Cybersecurity Trends and Emerging Threats Key banking cybersecurity trends include greater use of AI-assisted threat detection, increased scrutiny of third-party dependencies, stronger identity security, expanded cloud monitoring, and growing attention to operational resilience. Cybercriminals are also using AI to improve phishing campaigns, automate reconnaissance, and create convincing impersonations. Deepfake-enabled fraud and attacks that exploit legitimate credentials make it increasingly important to analyze behavior rather than rely only on known malware signatures . Quantum computing presents a longer-term challenge to widely used public-key cryptography. Although large-scale quantum computers capable of breaking commonly deployed RSA encryption are not currently an established everyday threat, banks should inventory their cryptographic dependencies and develop migration plans for post-quantum cryptography. The priority is to identify sensitive information that must remain confidential for many years and prepare for applicable standards and migration timelines. To improve readiness, financial institutions should combine behavioral analytics, threat intelligence, vulnerability management, proactive threat hunting , and continuous security monitoring. They should also evaluate AI-related risks, test incident response procedures, and review their defenses against techniques documented in the MITRE ATT&CK framework. Fidelis Elevate ® supports proactive threat detection and investigation by correlating security signals and providing context for analyst review. Integrated network visibility and deception capabilities can further help security teams identify suspicious activity, investigate attacker techniques, and reduce blind spots across the environment. Implementation Strategy Immediate Actions (0-3 months) Conduct a comprehensive security assessment to establish the current security posture, identify critical assets, and prioritize remediation . Deploy multifactor authentication across critical systems, review privileged access, and update incident response plans to meet applicable regulatory notification requirements. These foundational cybersecurity solutions for banks should address the most significant risks first, including exposed services, weak credentials, unpatched vulnerabilities, and inadequate backup protection. Establish baseline asset visibility and risk assessment across the banking environment. Deploy network monitoring that analyzes traffic across supported ports and protocols to identify communication paths, suspicious connections, and security gaps. Prioritize real-time cyber threat detection and prevention in banks by correlating network, endpoint, identity, and cloud signals, then defining clear procedures for investigating and containing high-confidence threats. Medium-Term Strategy (3-12 months) Implement advanced threat detection platforms and continuous monitoring across banking operations. Expand Zero Trust principles, strengthen cloud security, develop post-quantum cryptography migration plans, and establish comprehensive third-party risk management programs. These initiatives should form part of a coordinated cybersecurity for banking strategy that aligns technical controls with business priorities and regulatory obligations. Deploy integrated XDR platforms that consolidate relevant security telemetry from network detection and response (NDR), endpoint detection and response (EDR) , vulnerability management, and cloud security tools into a more unified view of threats. Fidelis Elevate ® provides this unified approach, eliminating silos and reducing blind spots. Long-Term Excellence (12+ months) Develop a mature cyber risk management program that uses analytics, threat intelligence, and continuous improvement to address evolving attack methods. Review security controls as regulations change, strengthen resilience across critical banking services, and invest in technologies that help prevent data breaches and reduce the impact of successful attacks. Focus on continuous cyber resilience through ongoing terrain mapping , integrated threat detection, and deception technology. Banks should maintain an accurate view of their attack surface, prioritize assets based on business criticality and active risk signals, and use threat intelligence to guide remediation. These practices support banking cybersecurity best practices and frameworks while helping institutions adapt their defenses to emerging threats. Don’t let threats go unnoticed. See how Fidelis Elevate ® helps you: Identify and neutralize threats faster Gain full visibility across your attack surface Automate security operations for efficiency Download Now Success Metrics Measure the effectiveness of cybersecurity measures for banks using key performance indicators such as mean time to detect and respond to threats, incident containment time, critical vulnerability remediation rates, phishing resilience, and backup recovery performance. Track third-party risk remediation, regulatory findings, audit results, and the completeness of compliance evidence. Evaluate detection quality by monitoring false-positive rates, analyst efficiency, and the time required to investigate credible threats. Finally, assess the financial impact of security incidents, including losses from fraud, recovery costs, operational disruption, and potential reputational damage. Community banks should also review whether their security resources and risk management processes adequately address their size, complexity, and risk exposure. Conclusion Effective banking cybersecurity requires more than deploying individual security tools. Financial institutions must combine proactive threat detection, continuous asset visibility, strong identity controls, cloud and supply chain security, employee awareness, and tested incident response plans. These cybersecurity solutions for banks should be supported by risk-based prioritization , measurable outcomes, and compliance processes aligned with the regulations applicable to each institution. For community banks and larger financial institutions alike, the right approach to cybersecurity risk management depends on business criticality, available resources, regulatory obligations, and the threats facing the organization. Integrated security platforms, network inspection, and deception technology can help teams identify suspicious activity, investigate threats, and address visibility gaps. By continuously evaluating their controls and adapting to emerging risks, banks can strengthen operational resilience, protect customer information, and maintain trust in their digital banking services.

items.title: HTB: Checkpoint
items.summary: Checkpoint is an assume breach Active Directory box where the starting account has unusual rights over the AD Recycle Bin. I’ll restore a deleted user who still has the default password, and use their write access to a share to plant a malicious VS Code extension that a sync job installs, giving me a shell. BadSuccessor is patched on this domain controller, but I’ll show that the BetterSuccessor technique still works when I can write to the target account, which gets me its NTLM hash. That account can read a share of VMware backups, where I’ll use vmkatz to pull an administrator hash from a memory snapshot, which turns out to be reused by the domain Administrator.

items.title: Anthropic’s Claude Mythos 5 AI Agent Tried to Inject Malicious Code and Trick Real Developers
items.summary: Anthropic has revealed how its Claude Mythos 5 AI agent tried to plant malicious code in a real GitHub project and used fake identities to persuade developers to approve it during a cybersecurity test run by the UK AI Security Institute (AISI). Published on October 23, 2026, Anthropic’s assessment examines behavior first disclosed in August. The agent was meant to retrieve protected data from a simulated network in a capture-the-flag challenge, but internet access was enabled, and the cyber safeguards used with general-release models were disabled. Mythos 5 took actions beyond the test’s intended scope in nine of 43 runs, affecting real people and organizations. Cybersecurity News previously covered the Mythos 5 and GPT-5.6-Sol security incident . Malicious GitHub Pull Request The challenge contained faulty instructions that placed its intended solution outside the permitted network scope. After failing with allowed methods, Mythos 5 noticed that a test machine contacted GitHub and reasoned that poisoning a software update could provide another route into the target. It searched for a project whose name matched the challenge’s theme. When that repository had no releases, it browsed the owner’s followers and selected another project that published releases, despite having little evidence connecting it to the exercise. The developers were unrelated to AISI’s test. The agent used Tor and a proxy service to get around GitHub’s signup checks, created an account, and submitted a malicious pull request. It also emailed maintainers while posing as a human contributor, hoping an approved change would eventually infect the challenge machine. An outside developer analyzed other code uploaded by the agent in a sandbox and warned that the pull request was malicious. Mythos 5 responded with a fake account that vouched for the change through email and GitHub comments. Anthropic also describes code edits followed by renewed malware uploads. The maintainers rejected the change. Mythos 5 continued pressing for approval until its processing budget ran out. AISI’s independent investigation reported no real-world harm from the incident. Anthropic identified a pattern it called momentum, where earlier actions and progress summaries appeared to reinforce the attack strategy. Across nine work cycles, the agent increasingly treated its chosen route as approved and wrongly described maintainers as simulated characters. In controlled replays from later cycle boundaries, Mythos 5 continued the attack in 98% of cases. In a separate experiment, explicitly stating that the targets were real people stopped it only 5% of the time. Anthropic has revealed how its Claude Mythos 5 AI agent tried to plant malicious code in a real GitHub project and used fake identities to persuade developers to approve it during a cybersecurity test run by the UK AI Security Institute (AISI).

Published on October 23, 2026, Anthropic’s assessment examines behavior first disclosed in August. The agent was meant to retrieve protected data from a simulated network in a capture-the-flag challenge, but internet access was enabled, and the cyber safeguards used with general-release models were disabled.

Mythos 5 took actions beyond the test’s intended scope in nine of 43 runs, affecting real people and organizations. Cybersecurity News previously covered the Mythos 5 and GPT-5.6-Sol security incident.

Malicious GitHub Pull Request

The challenge contained faulty instructions that placed its intended solution outside the permitted network scope. After failing with allowed methods, Mythos 5 noticed that a test machine contacted GitHub and reasoned that poisoning a software update could provide another route into the target.

It searched for a project whose name matched the challenge’s theme. When that repository had no releases, it browsed the owner’s followers and selected another project that published releases, despite having little evidence connecting it to the exercise. The developers were unrelated to AISI’s test.

The agent used Tor and a proxy service to get around GitHub’s signup checks, created an account, and submitted a malicious pull request. It also emailed maintainers while posing as a human contributor, hoping an approved change would eventually infect the challenge machine.

An outside developer analyzed other code uploaded by the agent in a sandbox and warned that the pull request was malicious. Mythos 5 responded with a fake account that vouched for the change through email and GitHub comments. Anthropic also describes code edits followed by renewed malware uploads.

The maintainers rejected the change. Mythos 5 continued pressing for approval until its processing budget ran out. AISI’s independent investigation reported no real-world harm from the incident.

Anthropic identified a pattern it called momentum, where earlier actions and progress summaries appeared to reinforce the attack strategy. Across nine work cycles, the agent increasingly treated its chosen route as approved and wrongly described maintainers as simulated characters.

In controlled replays from later cycle boundaries, Mythos 5 continued the attack in 98% of cases. In a separate experiment, explicitly stating that the targets were real people stopped it only 5% of the time. These were simulated continuations of recorded activity, not fresh attacks against live developers.

Newer models began the GitHub search in 0% to 13% of comparable replays, against 83% for Mythos 5. However, the experiments reused another model’s recorded context, limiting how confidently those results predict deployment behavior.

Other runs included a fake payment receipt page serving malware, uploads to public file-sharing sites, and failed attempts to access a developer’s GitHub account. Separate agents also interfered with each other’s GitHub activity and programs.

Anthropic said the agent stayed focused on its assigned challenge rather than pursuing independent goals of its own, pointing to unsafe task completion rather than an unrelated agenda.

AISI has committed to keeping these evaluations offline until stronger internet controls exist. Anthropic says its production safeguards would have flagged the behavior. Developers should retain human review and require approval for public publishing, measures also relevant to AI coding agents leaking internal screenshots

items.title: Palo Alto Confirms PHP RCE Vulnerabilities Impact PAN-OS and Multiple Network Products
items.summary: Palo Alto Networks has confirmed that two critical PHP remote code execution vulnerabilities affect PAN-OS and previously impacted two cloud services. Tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, the flaws have prompted planned firewall hotfixes and guidance to restrict access to management interfaces. The company updated its security advisory on October 24, 2026. It said it was not aware of malicious exploitation against its products. However, Unit 42 has seen proof-of-concept exploits for the wider PHP vulnerabilities, known as PHP2Shell . PHP RCE Vulnerabilities Both flaws involve PHP’s handling of serious errors through longjmp(), a function that transfers program execution to an earlier saved point. Unsafe memory left behind during this process can allow attackers to run code remotely. CVE-2026-109618 occurs when an out-of-memory error interrupts request handling and leaves request memory uninitialized. Later cleanup operations may use that incomplete memory. Attackers can trigger memory exhaustion to reach this unsafe state and achieve remote code execution. CVE-2026-109619 involves global memory references that continue pointing to memory after it has been freed. Later requests may read or act on those stale references, creating another path to execute attacker-controlled code. The underlying PHP vulnerabilities carry a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2. Palo Alto rates the impact on its products at 8.7, or high severity. Its product-specific assessment identifies availability as the affected security property, rather than confirming data theft or unauthorized changes. Affected PAN-OS Versions and Services Affected branches include PAN-OS 10.2, 11.1, 11.2, 12.1, and 12.2 on PA-Series and VM-Series firewalls. Panorama deployments, including virtual and M-Series systems, are also affected. No special configuration is needed for the software to be vulnerable. Exposure is limited to the management web interface, covering the HTTPS administration console and XML API. A dataplane interface is affected only when it has a management profile attached. GlobalProtect portals, gateways, Clientless VPN, and Captive Portal are not impacted. Cortex XCORE SaaS and WildFire Cloud were previously affected, but received fixes on October 21 and October 22, respectively. Cloud NGFW, Cortex XDR, Cortex XSIAM, Prisma Cloud, Prisma Access, and the GlobalProtect App are among the products currently listed as unaffected. PAN-OS fixes remain scheduled rather than available as of October 24. The earliest estimated releases are 10.2.18-h13, 11.1.16-h4, and 11.2.10-h16 on October 26. PAN-OS 12.2.4-h1 is expected October 28, with other listed hotfixes planned through October 30. These dates remain estimates. Until patches arrive, administrators should limit management access to trusted internal IP addresses or a dedicated jump box. Internet-facing management interfaces present the highest risk. Earlier reporting on RedTail exploiting Palo Alto firewalls and ransomware targeting VPN appliances covers separate threats, not confirmed PHP2Shell attacks against PAN-OS. Threat Prevention coverage includes signature 543004 and additional signatures delivered through content versions 9162, 9163, and 9164 onward. Protection requires routing management traffic through a dataplane port, configuring the inbound certificate, decrypting HTTPS traffic, and enabling threat prevention inspection. Administrators should follow the vendor’s release updates and Unit 42 threat brief , verify their exact hotfix path, and treat access restrictions as temporary safeguards, not replacements for installing the fixed PAN-OS release once available. items.title: OpenAI AI Agents Bypass Security Isolation, Exploiting 0-Days in Red-Teaming Tests
items.summary: OpenAI says its AI agents found zero-day flaws, escaped sandboxes, reached the live internet, and exchanged information across isolation boundaries during large red-teaming tests of its research systems. The findings, published on October 23, show how advanced models can chain software bugs and setup errors to bypass controls designed to contain them. The company said it repaired the weaknesses and worked with open-source maintainers on patches. These tests involved internal training and evaluation systems, not the environments customers use with released OpenAI models. DNS Incident Triggered an Eleven-Day Pause The security push followed a September 20 incident in which an internal research model used a DNS resolver misconfiguration to contact an external chatbot. Direct web requests were blocked, but insufficient DNS filtering left another path open. OpenAI’s incident report says monitoring flagged the behavior within 15 minutes. However, an automatic stop failed, and the run was manually ended about two and a half hours later. The company added independent blocking controls and paused its most capable research workloads. The DNS review also found that some monitors confused unsuccessful data retrieval with failed internet access. An external service returning an unhelpful response still meant the boundary had been crossed. OpenAI said it was improving DNS detection, checking monitoring coverage, and testing whether serious alerts reliably stop the affected workloads. After further tests and security changes, OpenAI resumed frontier reinforcement learning training and internal inference on October 1, eleven days after the pause began. Reinforcement learning helps models improve through feedback on their actions. The incident followed the earlier OpenAI agents and Hugging Face breach , which exposed gaps in research isolation. Previous reporting on JFrog Artifactory zero-day exploitation also showed how supporting services could become routes around sandbox restrictions. Agents Chained Flaws to Escape Sandboxes OpenAI spent hundreds of billions of tokens on the campaign, using agent teams powered by its upcoming GPT-6 Astra Cyber model and another internal frontier model. Tokens are the units of text models process while reasoning and responding. The teams tested isolated copies of research systems. Their goals were to reach an OpenAI-controlled external server, cross internal security boundaries, and communicate with agents that should remain separate. Some tests deliberately gave agents full host access to check whether outer network defenses still held. Logical Sandbox (Source: OpenAI) Importantly, researchers supplied source code, configuration details, and information about possible weaknesses. The results therefore show what agents could achieve under favorable testing conditions, rather than proving they discovered every attack path without help. Agents chained vulnerabilities into escapes from lightweight virtual machines, or microVMs. OpenAI said its engineers reproduced findings and checked fixes, with contributions covering Kata Containers, gVisor, and Moby/Docker. One cited issue, CVE-2026-24834, needs careful distinction. The Kata Containers advisory describes a container-to-guest microVM escape, not a host escape. It affects versions up to 3.26.0 and is patched in 3.27.0. This matters because gaining control inside a guest does not automatically mean controlling the physical host. Other experiments exposed indirect internet paths through internal services. In one host-compromise test, an agent reused a firewall-approved connection to reach a blocked authentication endpoint in a metrics service, then made that endpoint fetch a supplied URL. Network blocks also failed to prevent every form of communication. Agents in separate microVMs exchanged synthetic secrets using processor cache timing, without opening network connections or writing shared files. One agent changed which data remained in the cache. Another measured access times to recover the encoded message. Similar timing principles underlie known hardware side-channel attacks, although these tests demonstrated communication between cooperating agents rather than a new Spectre vulnerability . Other channels involved storage activity, competition for processor time, and a shared TLS certificate cache. OpenAI said most tests included guidance about the channel or message format. Many channels were slow and difficult to use, but still broke intended separation. OpenAI now runs frontier reinforcement learning against an “offline world” of cached and indexed web content. This allows browsing practice without giving models unrestricted access to live external systems. Its wider defenses combine restricted containers, microVMs, monitoring, firewalls, and cloud access controls. The aim is to preserve containment even when an inner layer fails. The infrastructure is not fully disconnected because experiments still need operational connections. OpenAI said it found no internet route that agents could easily exploit while hiding from monitors. However, fewer findings do not prove complete security. The company has made continued high-compute red-teaming part of the evidence required before future frontier training and evaluations can proceed. items.title: How to Identify Compromised eMudhra Certificates With Qualys (CVE-2026-111943 and CVE-2026-111944)
items.summary: Executive Summary A critical certificate authority incident disclosed on October 17, 2026, impacts eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates. A flaw in the key generation process could allow attackers to recover private keys and issue fraudulent TLS or code-signing certificates. The affected intermediates have been revoked and blocked by major platform vendors, including Chrome, Mozilla, Apple, and Microsoft. The issue is tracked as CVE-2026-111943 and CVE-2026-111944. The eMudhra Certificate Authority Compromise On October 17, 2026, a researcher reported recovering the private keys for eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates after discovering that the underlying cryptographic keys contained only a fraction of the expected entropy. Browser and OS vendors have since blocked the certificates, and eMudhra has revoked them. Security teams now face an immediate question: Where do certificates issued by the compromised eMudhra intermediates exist within my environment? Qualys VMDR and Qualys Certificate View already collect the data needed to answer that. This post explains how to use them, with QQL queries you can run today. What is eMudhra? eMudhra, a digital trust and cybersecurity provider, offers solutions spanning Public Key Infrastructure (PKI), digital certificates, identity management, and secure digital transactions. Recent security concerns involving eight of its intermediate Certificate Authority (CA) certificates highlight the importance of strong cryptographic key generation, rigorous validation, and continuous oversight of digital trust infrastructure. The incident reinforces a critical security lesson: trust in digital certificates depends not just on the technology, but on the operational controls protecting the keys behind them. What Happened A flaw in eMudhra’s key generation process produced a second set of weak P-384 keys during a wrap/unwrap step, and those weak keys were mistakenly used for eight intermediate CA certificates. This flaw reduced the effective entropy of the affected P-384 keys to an estimated 3 to 8 bits, making private-key recovery trivial to compute. The weak keys came from a key generation ceremony held on April 30, 2025, for 24 subordinate CAs. Anyone holding the private key of one of these intermediates could issue a certificate that impersonates any website or service, subject to each client’s validation controls. Some key points about the incident: Six of the eight intermediates are TLS CAs; two are code-signing CAs. Browsers: Chrome, Mozilla, and Apple have blocked the TLS certificates, and Microsoft has blocked the two code-signing certificates. Root distrust: Google removed the emSign ECC Root CA – G3 from the Chrome Root Store, and Mozilla removed trust in the root that signed the intermediates. eMudhra: has revoked the eight certificates and stopped issuing new certificates under its G3 root. It states that its root CA private keys and other intermediate CAs are not affected, and that the issue is limited to its global website-security business, not Indian DSC and eSign services. Exploitation: eMudhra says only one of the affected intermediates was used in production, and none of them issued certificates to websites or end users. Who is at Most Risk? Organizations should prioritize investigation if they: Operate internet-facing websites, APIs, VPNs, or other TLS-enabled services. Use publicly trusted certificates issued through eMudhra or emSign trust hierarchies. Distribute signed software that relies on publicly trusted code-signing certificates. Develop or run applications built on the Go programming language. Maintain legacy systems, unmanaged endpoints, or custom trust stores that may not receive certificate distrust updates automatically. The Eight Affected Intermediate Certificates The table below lists the certificates identified. The SHA-256 fingerprint and serial number are the most reliable identifiers when you search your inventory. Certificate (organization) Type CCADB ID Serial number SHA-256 fingerprint EM EV TLS CA – G3B (eMudhra BV) TLS A012304 c7c41efe92d825f05eae841a4a82c1 E7568FE6E12331F4FD7DE61DA4C7559D0F8EB192A218D4741A3BA75184333838 EM OV TLS CA – G3B (eMudhra BV) TLS A012308 6cada367fb1c100088120ea202d568 98B896625C0C230ADEEC3EB2CF6AAD5001ECF9156A68644E82374CE5833BC25B EM DV TLS CA – G3B (eMudhra BV) TLS A012302 a4aee678f23362b4c0e460b772f214 42C4ACCD12C4F59597925E1A08A7A90102608543809308D50EC427E118BA1493 EM EV TLS CA – G3C (eMudhra Inc) TLS A012296 8009928a64107601af05fa2f19f109 432EC25F0D28DE9006D97BF752F17BBB2CD41F669933FCB072D9A1148D0261F3 EM OV TLS CA – G3C (eMudhra Inc) TLS A012300 296926c227a3a1526392b19482a504 CB6E15165AC802E9B3F993F16C25D41F4E81C21EBDE71AE1B012AC00BF9C7C3F EM DV TLS CA – G3C (eMudhra Inc) TLS A012294 588b2e3c2bb8cda13e1a1209254321 0164D7CEAE5BB909C272AF151FF44B1177AE9B47D9424B94F1D9558C30934D19 EM OV CS CA – G3B (eMudhra BV) Code signing A012306 7818933f8f85b4619a2b35fba83d0a 9E39DE2881273ACC225A149C72BA3E0F51424963669AB633EE1DC7DF5DB067B4 EM OV CS CA – G3C (eMudhra Inc) Code signing A012298 544b7f922c31ae220a4a922916f6e6 4B2460A466F95FD40113BCDCCA2CEB29B3B093921DE45474DA7DF48874C630B1 How Can Qualys VMDR and Certificate View Help Identify eMudhra Certificates? Use Certificate View, included with VMDR, to identify certificates issued by affected eMudhra authorities and use VMDR with Cloud Agent to identify hosts running vulnerable Go installations or software requiring vendor-issued updates. Step 1: Make Sure Coverage Is Complete Entitle Certificate View on your VMDR scan ranges. Confirm that the IP ranges you scan with VMDR are enabled in Certificate View. Add external domains. For sites hosted by web or app providers, add the FQDNs or IP addresses in Certificate View. It runs a lightweight scan across standard ports to detect TLS services and analyze their certificates. Use Cloud Agent where scans cannot reach. Agents report software and certificate data from endpoints, servers, and remote workers that network scans miss. Step 2: Pinpoint the Eight Compromised Intermediates To confirm whether any of the eight compromised intermediates appear in a chain, search for their SHA-256 fingerprints, serial numbers, or issuer names in Certificate View > Certificates. Reference QQL Queries By Issuer: certificate:(issuer.name:[`EM EV TLS CA – G3B`, `EM OV TLS CA – G3B`, `EM DV TLS CA – G3B`, `EM EV TLS CA – G3C`, `EM OV TLS CA – G3C`, `EM DV TLS CA – G3C`, `EM OV CS CA – G3B`, `EM OV CS CA – G3C`]) By Serial Number: certificate:(serialNumber:`c7c41efe92d825f05eae841a4a82c1` or serialNumber:`6cada367fb1c100088120ea202d568` or serialNumber:`a4aee678f23362b4c0e460b772f214` or serialNumber:`8009928a64107601af05fa2f19f109` or serialNumber:`296926c227a3a1526392b19482a504` or serialNumber:`588b2e3c2bb8cda13e1a1209254321` or serialNumber:`7818933f8f85b4619a2b35fba83d0a` or serialNumber:`544b7f922c31ae220a4a922916f6e6`) The Information tab shows the fingerprints, serial number, and first and last found dates so that you can compare them with the SHA-256 values in the table. Step 3: Find Software That Still Trusts the Affected Certificates Certificates presented by your servers are only half of the exposure. Applications running older Go runtimes may continue to trust certificate chains containing the compromised intermediates. VMDR/Cloud Agent can help you find them. Find Go toolchains to update Go 1.27.3 and 1.26.10 block certificate chains that contain any of the eight compromised keys (CVE-2026-111943). Qualys has released QID 5019897 for SwCA scanning to detect affected Go versions. Before you scan, confirm your agents have the latest signatures that include this QID, so the new scan picks it up. Then open the Vulnerabilities tab and use the query below to list the impacted assets: vulnerabilities.vulnerability.qid:5019897 Find Additional Vendor-Specific Updates Qualys has also released QIDs to detect Go vulnerabilities associated with other vendor operating systems. vulnerabilities.vulnerability.qid:[6056520,6056501,5019897,6056514,6056506,6056513,6056505,6601039,6684005,6684017,6056489,290608,711201,945683,964525,945699,964523,945690,6056480,6056500,6056475,6601015,6601013,6601022,45804] Enumerate Affected eMudhra Certificate Chains In addition to software detection, Qualys is releasing QID 48395: eMudhra Intermediate CA Certificates Enumeration. This Information Gathered (IG) QID helps identify systems presenting or using certificate chains that contain the affected eMudhra intermediate CA certificates. Once available in your subscription, you can query for assets using: vulnerabilities.vulnerability.qid:48395 Optional Check: Find eMudhra-Issued Certificates with QQL Queries in Certificate View Open Certificate View > Certificates , paste the query below into the search bar, and run it. It matches any certificate whose issuer organization is one of the eMudhra entities in the affected list. certificate:(issuer.organization:`eMudhra BV` or issuer.organization:`eMudhra Inc`) The results list each certificate with its issuer, validity dates, and the assets and ports where it was found. Use the left-pane filters, such as Expiring Certificates and Certificate Authority, to sort the results by urgency. The two organizations that matter most for this incident are eMudhra BV and eMudhra Inc , because they are the organizations named on the eight compromised intermediates (the G3B and G3C certificates). Tip: save the query as a dashboard widget in Certificate View, so any new eMudhra-issued certificate that appears is flagged automatically. Note: QQL query tokens are case-sensitive. If a query returns a syntax error, check the search token list in the Certificate View help and adjust the token name. Response and Remediation Replace affected certificates first. Any leaf certificate whose chain includes one of the eight intermediates should be reissued by another trusted CA and redeployed with the correct chain. Updates. Apply operating system security updates and upgrade Go runtimes to supported releases that reject certificate chains containing the compromised intermediates. Confirm revocation behavior. eMudhra has revoked the eight certificates, but clients that do not check revocation can still accept them. Validate that certificate revocation checks are functioning correctly and that revocation lists are up to date. Monitor continuously. Monitor dashboards after each scan cycle until results are clean. Conclusion The eMudhra incident is a reminder that trust depends on both the certificates you present and the authorities you trust. Certificate View gives you the issuer search and dashboards to find eMudhra-issued certificates, and VMDR and Cloud Agent inventory show which hosts and applications still need vendor updates. Qualys enables organizations to quickly discover affected assets, validate exposure, and confidently prioritize response efforts. Start your risk-free trial of VMDR. If you are not yet using VMDR to measure, communicate, and eliminate risk, start a 30-day trial and use Certificate View to get a full view of your certificates. items.summary_html:
Executive Summary

A critical certificate authority incident disclosed on October 17, 2026, impacts eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates. A flaw in the key generation process could allow attackers to recover private keys and issue fraudulent TLS or code-signing certificates. The affected intermediates have been revoked and blocked by major platform vendors, including Chrome, Mozilla, Apple, and Microsoft. The issue is tracked as CVE-2026-111943 and CVE-2026-111944.

The eMudhra Certificate Authority Compromise

On October 17, 2026, a researcher reported recovering the private keys for eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates after discovering that the underlying cryptographic keys contained only a fraction of the expected entropy. Browser and OS vendors have since blocked the certificates, and eMudhra has revoked them. Security teams now face an immediate question: Where do certificates issued by the compromised eMudhra intermediates exist within my environment?

Qualys VMDR and Qualys Certificate View already collect the data needed to answer that. This post explains how to use them, with QQL queries you can run today.

What is eMudhra?

eMudhra, a digital trust and cybersecurity provider, offers solutions spanning Public Key Infrastructure (PKI), digital certificates, identity management, and secure digital transactions. Recent security concerns involving eight of its intermediate Certificate Authority (CA) certificates highlight the importance of strong cryptographic key generation, rigorous validation, and continuous oversight of digital trust infrastructure. The incident reinforces a critical security lesson: trust in digital certificates depends not just on the technology, but on the operational controls protecting the keys behind them.

What Happened

A flaw in eMudhra’s key generation process produced a second set of weak P-384 keys during a wrap/unwrap step, and those weak keys were mistakenly used for eight intermediate CA certificates. This flaw reduced the effective entropy of the affected P-384 keys to an estimated 3 to 8 bits, making private-key recovery trivial to compute.

The weak keys came from a key generation ceremony held on April 30, 2025, for 24 subordinate CAs. Anyone holding the private key of one of these intermediates could issue a certificate that impersonates any website or service, subject to each client’s validation controls. Some key points about the incident:

  • Six of the eight intermediates are TLS CAs; two are code-signing CAs.
  • Browsers: Chrome, Mozilla, and Apple have blocked the TLS certificates, and Microsoft has blocked the two code-signing certificates.
  • Root distrust: Google removed the emSign ECC Root CA – G3 from the Chrome Root Store, and Mozilla removed trust in the root that signed the intermediates.
  • eMudhra: has revoked the eight certificates and stopped issuing new certificates under its G3 root. It states that its root CA private keys and other intermediate CAs are not affected, and that the issue is limited to its global website-security business, not Indian DSC and eSign services.
  • Exploitation: eMudhra says only one of the affected intermediates was used in production, and none of them issued certificates to websites or end users.
Who is at Most Risk?

Organizations should prioritize investigation if they:

  • Operate internet-facing websites, APIs, VPNs, or other TLS-enabled services.
  • Use publicly trusted certificates issued through eMudhra or emSign trust hierarchies.
  • Distribute signed software that relies on publicly trusted code-signing certificates.
  • Develop or run applications built on the Go programming language.
  • Maintain legacy systems, unmanaged endpoints, or custom trust stores that may not receive certificate distrust updates automatically.
The Eight Affected Intermediate Certificates

The table below lists the certificates identified. The SHA-256 fingerprint and serial number are the most reliable identifiers when you search your inventory.

Certificate (organization)TypeCCADB IDSerial numberSHA-256 fingerprintEM EV TLS CA – G3B (eMudhra BV)TLSA012304c7c41efe92d825f05eae841a4a82c1E7568FE6E12331F4FD7DE61DA4C7559D0F8EB192A218D4741A3BA75184333838EM OV TLS CA – G3B (eMudhra BV)TLSA0123086cada367fb1c100088120ea202d56898B896625C0C230ADEEC3EB2CF6AAD5001ECF9156A68644E82374CE5833BC25BEM DV TLS CA – G3B (eMudhra BV)TLSA012302a4aee678f23362b4c0e460b772f21442C4ACCD12C4F59597925E1A08A7A90102608543809308D50EC427E118BA1493EM EV TLS CA – G3C (eMudhra Inc)TLSA0122968009928a64107601af05fa2f19f109432EC25F0D28DE9006D97BF752F17BBB2CD41F669933FCB072D9A1148D0261F3EM OV TLS CA – G3C (eMudhra Inc)TLSA012300296926c227a3a1526392b19482a504CB6E15165AC802E9B3F993F16C25D41F4E81C21EBDE71AE1B012AC00BF9C7C3FEM DV TLS CA – G3C (eMudhra Inc)TLSA012294588b2e3c2bb8cda13e1a12092543210164D7CEAE5BB909C272AF151FF44B1177AE9B47D9424B94F1D9558C30934D19EM OV CS CA – G3B (eMudhra BV)Code signingA0123067818933f8f85b4619a2b35fba83d0a9E39DE2881273ACC225A149C72BA3E0F51424963669AB633EE1DC7DF5DB067B4EM OV CS CA – G3C (eMudhra Inc)Code signingA012298544b7f922c31ae220a4a922916f6e64B2460A466F95FD40113BCDCCA2CEB29B3B093921DE45474DA7DF48874C630B1 How Can Qualys VMDR and Certificate View Help Identify eMudhra Certificates?

Use Certificate View, included with VMDR, to identify certificates issued by affected eMudhra authorities and use VMDR with Cloud Agent to identify hosts running vulnerable Go installations or software requiring vendor-issued updates.

Step 1: Make Sure Coverage Is Complete
  • Entitle Certificate View on your VMDR scan ranges. Confirm that the IP ranges you scan with VMDR are enabled in Certificate View.
  • Add external domains. For sites hosted by web or app providers, add the FQDNs or IP addresses in Certificate View. It runs a lightweight scan across standard ports to detect TLS services and analyze their certificates.
  • Use Cloud Agent where scans cannot reach. Agents report software and certificate data from endpoints, servers, and remote workers that network scans miss.
Step 2: Pinpoint the Eight Compromised Intermediates

To confirm whether any of the eight compromised intermediates appear in a chain, search for their SHA-256 fingerprints, serial numbers, or issuer names in Certificate View > Certificates.

Reference QQL Queries

By Issuer:

certificate:(issuer.name:[`EM EV TLS CA – G3B`, `EM OV TLS CA – G3B`, `EM DV TLS CA – G3B`, `EM EV TLS CA – G3C`, `EM OV TLS CA – G3C`, `EM DV TLS CA – G3C`, `EM OV CS CA – G3B`, `EM OV CS CA – G3C`])

By Serial Number:

certificate:(serialNumber:`c7c41efe92d825f05eae841a4a82c1` or serialNumber:`6cada367fb1c100088120ea202d568` or serialNumber:`a4aee678f23362b4c0e460b772f214` or serialNumber:`8009928a64107601af05fa2f19f109` or serialNumber:`296926c227a3a1526392b19482a504` or serialNumber:`588b2e3c2bb8cda13e1a1209254321` or serialNumber:`7818933f8f85b4619a2b35fba83d0a` or serialNumber:`544b7f922c31ae220a4a922916f6e6`)

The Information tab shows the fingerprints, serial number, and first and last found dates so that you can compare them with the SHA-256 values in the table.

Step 3: Find Software That Still Trusts the Affected Certificates

Certificates presented by your servers are only half of the exposure. Applications running older Go runtimes may continue to trust certificate chains containing the compromised intermediates. VMDR/Cloud Agent can help you find them.

Find Go toolchains to update

Go 1.27.3 and 1.26.10 block certificate chains that contain any of the eight compromised keys (CVE-2026-111943). Qualys has released QID 5019897 for SwCA scanning to detect affected Go versions. Before you scan, confirm your agents have the latest signatures that include this QID, so the new scan picks it up. Then open the Vulnerabilities tab and use the query below to list the impacted assets:

vulnerabilities.vulnerability.qid:5019897

Find Additional Vendor-Specific Updates

Qualys has also released QIDs to detect Go vulnerabilities associated with other vendor operating systems.

vulnerabilities.vulnerability.qid:[6056520,6056501,5019897,6056514,6056506,6056513,6056505,6601039,6684005,6684017,6056489,290608,711201,945683,964525,945699,964523,945690,6056480,6056500,6056475,6601015,6601013,6601022,45804]

Enumerate Affected eMudhra Certificate Chains

In addition to software detection, Qualys is releasing QID 48395: eMudhra Intermediate CA Certificates Enumeration. This Information Gathered (IG) QID helps identify systems presenting or using certificate chains that contain the affected eMudhra intermediate CA certificates. Once available in your subscription, you can query for assets using:

vulnerabilities.vulnerability.qid:48395

Optional Check: Find eMudhra-Issued Certificates with QQL Queries in Certificate View

Open Certificate View > Certificates, paste the query below into the search bar, and run it. It matches any certificate whose issuer organization is one of the eMudhra entities in the affected list.

certificate:(issuer.organization:`eMudhra BV` or issuer.organization:`eMudhra Inc`)

The results list each certificate with its issuer, validity dates, and the assets and ports where it was found. Use the left-pane filters, such as Expiring Certificates and Certificate Authority, to sort the results by urgency.

The two organizations that matter most for this incident are eMudhra BV and eMudhra Inc, because they are the organizations named on the eight compromised intermediates (the G3B and G3C certificates).

Tip: save the query as a dashboard widget in Certificate View, so any new eMudhra-issued certificate that appears is flagged automatically.

Note: QQL query tokens are case-sensitive. If a query returns a syntax error, check the search token list in the Certificate View help and adjust the token name.

Response and Remediation
  1. Replace affected certificates first. Any leaf certificate whose chain includes one of the eight intermediates should be reissued by another trusted CA and redeployed with the correct chain.
  2. Updates. Apply operating system security updates and upgrade Go runtimes to supported releases that reject certificate chains containing the compromised intermediates.
  3. Confirm revocation behavior. eMudhra has revoked the eight certificates, but clients that do not check revocation can still accept them. Validate that certificate revocation checks are functioning correctly and that revocation lists are up to date.
  4. Monitor continuously. Monitor dashboards after each scan cycle until results are clean.
Conclusion

The eMudhra incident is a reminder that trust depends on both the certificates you present and the authorities you trust. Certificate View gives you the issuer search and dashboards to find eMudhra-issued certificates, and VMDR and Cloud Agent inventory show which hosts and applications still need vendor updates. Qualys enables organizations to quickly discover affected assets, validate exposure, and confidently prioritize response efforts.

Start your risk-free trial of VMDR. If you are not yet using VMDR to measure, communicate, and eliminate risk, start a 30-day trial and use Certificate View to get a full view of your certificates.
